opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I've become a pretty heavy user, and I think a lot of founders have. When you're running a company, especially a hardware startup where the decisions are expensive and the cycles are long, you don't always have someone available at eleven at night to argue with you about a go-to-market plan or a pricing model. A chatbot is always there, it's patient, and it'll engage with whatever half-formed idea you throw at it.

Where I find it most valuable is in pressure-testing. I'll lay out a strategy and ask it to poke holes: what am I missing, what would a competitor do in response, what would a skeptical investor say? It's very good at surfacing the second- and third-order considerations you might gloss over when you're excited about something. It's also good at structuring messy thinking. You dump a bunch of thoughts in, and it gives you back a framework you can actually react to.

But I'm careful about a few things. First, these models tend to be agreeable. If you frame a question in a way that signals what you want to hear, there's a good chance you'll hear it. So I've learned to deliberately ask it to argue the other side, or to assume my plan fails and explain why. Second, the model doesn't have the context that really matters: the relationships, the nuance of a specific customer conversation, the internal dynamics of your team, what's actually happening in a market that moves every few months. That's where human judgment and real advisors still carry the weight.

So I'd put it this way: it's an excellent sparring partner and a terrific first-draft thinker, but it's not a decision-maker. The accountability still sits with you. Used that way, it makes you sharper and faster. Used as an oracle, it can give you false confidence. And as someone who builds infrastructure for inference, I'll add that the fact that people are using it this way, constantly, for long, reasoning-heavy conversations, is exactly why the cost and efficiency of serving these models matters so much.

fable-5.1.text:
Sid Sheth: I use them, honestly, more than I expected to. But I'd frame it carefully. A chatbot is a very good sounding board and a very poor decision-maker, and the mistake people make is confusing the two.

Where they're genuinely useful is in the early, messy part of thinking. When I'm trying to articulate a position, say, where we should sit in the inference market versus the big incumbents, I'll write out my reasoning and ask the model to attack it. Where are the holes? What would a skeptical investor say? What's the strongest version of the opposing view? It does that well, because it has absorbed an enormous amount of how people argue about strategy. It's like having a tireless, well-read colleague who never gets offended when you tell them their point was weak.

Where they fall down is on anything that depends on information the model doesn't have, and in a company like ours, that's most of what matters. The model doesn't know what a customer told us in a meeting last week. It doesn't know that a particular supplier is slipping, or that a competitor's roadmap is six months behind what they're saying publicly. It doesn't know which of my engineers I trust on a schedule and which ones are optimistic. Strategy lives in that proprietary context, and if you ask a chatbot a strategic question without feeding it that context, you get a very fluent summary of conventional wisdom. Conventional wisdom is exactly what you don't want when you're a startup. If the obvious answer were right, the incumbent would already be doing it.

There's also a subtler problem, which is that these systems are agreeable. If you present a plan with conviction, they tend to find reasons it's good. So I've learned to never ask "is this a good idea." I ask "give me three reasons this fails," or I present two options neutrally and ask it to argue each side. You have to design the prompt against the model's tendency to please you.

So my assessment is: as a thinking partner, as a way to pressure-test and sharpen an argument, they're excellent and I'd encourage any executive to use them that way. As an oracle, as something that tells you what to do, they're actively dangerous, because the confidence of the output has nothing to do with the quality of the judgment behind it. The judgment still has to be yours.

astra-6.text:
I think they can be very useful, particularly for getting your thoughts organized and exploring different options. You can lay out a business problem, ask for a counterargument, and see whether there’s something you’ve overlooked. That’s a valuable sounding board.

But you have to be careful about treating a convincing answer as a correct answer. A chatbot may not have the context that really matters: your customers, your team’s capabilities, or the constraints you’re operating under. And if it simply reinforces your assumptions, it’s not helping you very much.

So I’d use it to challenge a strategy. Ask, “Why might this fail? What assumptions am I making? What evidence would change my mind?” Then take those questions back to your team and your customers. It can improve the thinking, but the judgment and accountability still sit with you.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re useful as a way to pressure-test your thinking. You can lay out a business idea and ask, “What assumptions am I making? Where could this fail? What would a competitor do?” That can help you explore questions you might otherwise miss.

But you have to be careful about treating a coherent answer as a correct answer. A chatbot may not have the context of your customers, your team, or the constraints you’re operating under. And if it simply agrees with you, it’s not much of a sounding board. So I’d use it to generate alternatives and challenge assumptions, then validate those ideas with customers and real-world evidence. The judgment and accountability still sit with you.
